10. Correlation Analysis

11. Key Findings – 10-Point Summary

  1. The portfolio contains 678,013 policies with 358,499 policy-years of exposure, and the severity file holds 26,639 individual claim amounts.
  2. Claim counts are heavily zero-inflated: 95.0% of policies report no claim, and the maximum is 16 claims on one policy.
  3. The overall claim frequency is 0.1007 claims per policy-year with a variance/mean ratio of 1.08, i.e. over-dispersion that favours Negative Binomial or zero-inflated count models.
  4. Exposure is unequal: 75.0% of policies are observed for less than one year (median 0.49), so exposure must enter frequency models as an offset.
  5. Claim severity is highly right-skewed (mean 2,279 vs median 1,172, skewness 109.6), indicating a heavy tail suited to Gamma, Log-normal or Pareto-type models.
  6. Large losses dominate the total cost: the top 1% of claims make up 38.0% of the total claim amount, so large-claim capping or a separate tail model should be considered.
  7. Bonus-Malus is the strongest frequency driver: the frequency in the highest band (151+: 0.568) is 7.1x that of drivers at the minimum level 50 (0.080).
  8. Driver age has a U-shaped effect: young drivers (18-20) show the highest frequency (0.249), while the lowest is in the 31-40 band (0.090).
  9. Urbanisation raises risk: frequency rises from 0.083 in the most rural density quintile to 0.125 in the most urban; Area F has the highest frequency (0.139) and Area A the lowest (0.082).
  10. Data are clean (no missing values), but 195 severity records lack a matching policy and 9,117 claiming policies have a ClaimNb inconsistent with the severity file; the frequency–severity Spearman correlation among claimants is 0.031, supporting a joint modelling approach. (Most common brand: B12; region: Centre; diesel vs regular frequency: 0.098 vs 0.104.)
